p: The second war of the twentieth century will be, by every measure, the greatest catastrophe in the recorded history of mankind. The Encyclopaedia estimates its dead at some seventy to eighty-five million, the greater part of them not soldiers but civilians: men, women and children killed by bombing, by famine, by massacre, and by a deliberate plan of extermination so monstrous that I have hesitated for many nights before setting it down. I shall set it down, because a historian who flinches from the worst of the record betrays the dead.

Germany, defeated, humiliated and then ruined by an inflation in which its money became worthless, and later by a world-wide collapse of trade that threw millions out of work, will turn in its despair to a party of fanatics, the National Socialists, or Nazis, led by an Austrian former corporal named Adolf Hitler. He will preach that Germany was betrayed, not defeated; that the Jews, in particular, were the authors of all its misfortunes; and that the German race must conquer living space in the east. He will become Chancellor in January nineteen thirty-three, destroy all opposition within months, and begin to rearm. In Italy, a former socialist journalist, Benito Mussolini, will already rule as a dictator; in Japan, the army will seize control of the government and invade China. Britain and France, horrified by the memory of the last war, will try to satisfy Hitler with concessions, and at Munich in nineteen thirty-eight will allow him to take part of Czechoslovakia. The British Prime Minister, Mr Neville Chamberlain, will return to London declaring peace for our time. Within a year, on the first of September nineteen thirty-nine, Germany will invade Poland, and Britain and France will declare war.

In the spring of nineteen-forty, the German armies, using tanks and aeroplanes in swift combination, will overrun Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and France in a few weeks. The British army will escape from the beaches of Dunkirk in a fleet of warships and small boats. Britain, under a new Prime Minister, Mr Winston Churchill, the grandson of a Duke of Marlborough and, I learn, at this moment an infant of one year, will fight on alone; and in the summer and autumn of that year, the young pilots of the Royal Air Force will defeat the German air force over southern England, and the invasion will be abandoned. London and other cities will be bombed for months, and the people will shelter in the stations of the underground railway, which I am glad to say is already being built.

In June nineteen forty-one, Hitler will invade the Soviet Union with the largest army ever assembled, and reach the gates of Moscow. In December, Japan will attack the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, in the Hawaiian Islands, and the United States will enter the war. The tide will turn in nineteen forty-two and forty-three: at Midway in the Pacific, at El Alamein in Egypt, and above all at Stalingrad on the river Volga, where a German army of a quarter of a million men will be surrounded and destroyed in the winter. The war in the east will be fought with a savagery without precedent; the Soviet Union alone will lose something like twenty-seven million dead. On the sixth of June, nineteen forty-four, the British, Americans and Canadians will land on the coast of Normandy. Germany will surrender in May nineteen forty-five, a week after Hitler kills himself in a bunker beneath his ruined capital.

Behind the armies, in the conquered lands of the east, the Nazis will carry out the murder of some six million Jews, two-thirds of the Jews of Europe, together with great numbers of Roma people, of the disabled, of Poles, of Soviet prisoners and of others. At first they will be shot beside pits they have been made to dig. Then, from nineteen forty-two, they will be carried in railway wagons, from every corner of occupied Europe, to camps built for the purpose, at places whose names the Encyclopaedia records, Auschwitz, Treblinka, Sobibor and others, and killed with poison gas, in chambers disguised as bathhouses, and their bodies burned. It will be done by a modern state, with the methods of a modern industry, its railways, its paperwork and its chemistry, by men many of whom went home in the evening to their families. The world will come to call it the Holocaust, from a Greek word meaning a burnt offering, or the Shoah, a Hebrew word meaning catastrophe.

I have spent my life studying cruelty, and I believed that I knew its whole range. I was wrong. I can only say, with the historians of the future, that it happened, that it was done by human beings, and that the first duty of history is to make sure that it is never forgotten or denied.

The war will end in the Pacific with a new weapon. Early in the twentieth century, men of science will discover that the atom, which our chemists believe to be the smallest and indivisible particle of matter, as its Greek name implies, is not indivisible at all, and that within its tiny centre are locked forces of inconceivable power. In nineteen thirty-eight, two German chemists, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, will find that the atom of a heavy metal called uranium can be split, and their former colleague Lise Meitner, a Jewish physicist who has fled Germany, with her nephew Otto Frisch, will explain what has happened and calculate the energy released. Scientists who had fled the Nazis, among them Albert Einstein, will warn the American President, Franklin Roosevelt, that Germany might build a bomb from it.

The Americans, with the help of the British, will then undertake the greatest scientific and industrial project ever attempted, which will be called the Manhattan Project, employing at its height some hundred and thirty thousand people, at secret cities in Tennessee, Washington and New Mexico, under a general named Leslie Groves and a brilliant physicist, Robert Oppenheimer. On the sixteenth of July, nineteen forty-five, in the desert of New Mexico, they will explode the first atomic bomb. Oppenheimer will later say that a line from the Hindu scripture called the Bhagavad Gita came into his mind: now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.

On the sixth of August, nineteen forty-five, a single bomb will destroy the Japanese city of Hiroshima, and on the ninth another will destroy Nagasaki, the old port where the Portuguese first traded. Together they will kill, by the end of that year, perhaps a hundred and fifty to two hundred thousand people. Japan will surrender within days. Whether the bombs were necessary to end the war, or saved more lives than they took, the historians of the future still dispute with great bitterness.

After the war, the victors will found the United Nations, try the leaders of Germany and Japan for crimes against humanity, and set down a Universal Declaration of Human Rights. But they will also, within a few years, both possess the atomic bomb and point it at one another. For the first time since the beginning of this history, mankind will hold in its hands the means to destroy itself entirely. The Titan who stole fire, I think, would understand.
